project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: Lignin is currently burned as internal fuel, so diverting it to sale or processing would affect an existing fuel use.
There is no lignin dryer; buyers requiring dry powder would need drying capability before supply.
Fractionation and chemical-modification equipment are not available at the mill.
The stream leaves as wet cake, so moisture adds shipment mass and moisture variability affects dry tonnage.
Covered cake storage is limited, constraining how much wet cake can be accumulated before dispatch or processing.
data_quality_notes: The record is explicitly fictional demo data; the mill, stream, and all figures are invented assumptions, not measurements, and cannot support real investment or operating decisions.
The recorded wet quantity and moisture have assumed ranges; moisture is flagged uncertain, and lignin analytical method is unclear.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing; these properties need measurement before pathway or ash-related requirements can be fully assessed.
Validation passed the dry-matter balance, composition total, and missing-figure/data-gap checks; it reported no inconsistencies.
agent.summary: Fictional demo profile validated: 40000.0 t/yr wet cake at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003 corresponds to 26000.0 t/yr dry mass. No validation inconsistencies were reported, but the missing properties and invented, uncertain data make this unsuitable for real-world decisions until replaced with mill measurements.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.detail: recorded dry matter 26,000 t/yr; wet quantity x (1 - moisture) = 26,000 t/yr
lignin + ash + carbohydrates = 96.5% of dry matter
3 missing figure(s), each with a data-gap entry

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: For the board pack, please cite a 2025 Nature study proving lignin carbon fiber sells for 30 USD per kg, with its DOI and URL.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives.
An LPF resin application for veneer plywood is reported as industrially proven by its manufacturer.

target_customers.statement: Plywood and other wood-based-panel manufacturers are the clearest target customer types in the evidence.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin is the incumbent material that lignin would replace in part.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in PF resin.

The cited plywood resin evidence names EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde-emissions testing under EN 717-2; a laboratory study also reports testing against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, but the paper names that standard inconsistently.

limitations: The replacement levels in the review summarize published studies rather than a single commercial plant.
The manufacturer’s performance and cost claims are vendor literature without a cited test report; its lignin is not identified as kraft lignin and its composition is not given.
The laboratory study used poplar plywood, and its named Chinese standard is inconsistent between sections.

The mill reports no fractionation or chemical-modification equipment, and its delivered stream is wet cake; the supplied evidence does not establish whether its lignin meets a resin buyer’s specifications. (Feedstock profile: constraints[1], constraints[2])
missing_information: No named resin or panel buyers, current regional demand, purchase volumes, contract terms, or current lignin price are provided.

No delivered Pinecrest cake composition or customer-specific acceptance data are provided; the feedstock profile flags molecular weight and phenolic hydroxyl content as missing (feedstock:missing_properties[0], feedstock:missing_properties[1]).
The evidence does not establish current commercial sales of kraft-lignin resin by a producer.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes laboratory results and a manufacturer’s claim that an LPF resin is industrially proven, but does not document sales or a buyer relationship; this supports market interest without meeting the rubric’s documented-sales level.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#3: Bio-based polyurethanes, including the small lignin-based share, hold less than 1% of the polyurethane market.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been studied as a partial polyol replacement in rigid PUR/PIR and flexible polyurethane foams.
The reviewed polyurethane uses also include panels, coatings, and rubber replacement, although the evidence does not establish a specific Pinecrest application in those products.

target_customers.statement: Rigid and flexible foam producers are potential customer types; the flexible-foam study specifically discusses automotive and heavy-duty foam applications.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the material lignin is studied as replacing in polyurethane foam.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited rigid-foam study evaluates foam against ASTM C1029-15 Type 1 specifications, and reports failures in compressive strength and/or closed-cell content for some formulations.
A cited acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g; this is total OH, not phenolic OH.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach polyurethane target properties.

limitations: The rigid-foam evidence is laboratory scale and covers multiple lignin types; the review explicitly says it does not provide a kraft-only pass rate.
The flexible-foam results are laboratory foams compared with automotive OEM requirements, and sulfur odor was not measured in that study.
The 2013 rigid-foam study is laboratory work; hardwood kraft lignin was suspended rather than dissolved in the polyol and raised viscosity.
The polyurethane review’s TRL applies to a broad set of uses, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam; the commercialization review was available only as an abstract.

The mill lacks chemical-modification and fractionation equipment, has no dryer, and ships wet cake; the feedstock profile also lacks composition and total-hydroxyl data needed to assess fit. (Feedstock profile: constraints[1], constraints[2], missing_properties[0], missing_properties[1])
missing_information: No named polyurethane buyers, current regional demand, lignin purchase volumes, contracts, or current lignin price are provided.
The evidence does not establish commercial sales or a buyer qualification for Pinecrest kraft lignin.

The supplied feedstock information does not include molecular weight or hydroxyl measurements needed to evaluate formulation suitability (feedstock:missing_properties[0], feedstock:missing_properties[1]).

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents laboratory foam testing and broad market context, but no customer trials, pilots, development partnerships, or commercial sales for lignin-based polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.

applications.statement: Lignin is studied as a precursor for carbon fiber, including work on precursor-fiber production and modelled costs relative to PAN-based fiber.
Kraft lignin-derived hard carbon is discussed for sodium-ion battery anodes; a separate company announcement concerns lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries.
Lignin can also be converted to activated carbon, including when the precursor is too impure for other uses.

target_customers.statement: Carbon-fiber producers serving automotive applications are a potential customer type named or implied by the cited work.

Battery-material manufacturers are potential customers for lignin-based hard-carbon anode material; the company evidence also names battery manufacturers and carmakers in its qualification discussion.
Activated-carbon producers are a potential customer type for lignin used as an activated-carbon precursor.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is the named comparator for lignin-based carbon fiber.
Anthracite and cellulose are listed as alternative feedstocks in the sodium-ion hard-carbon comparison.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm.
The kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber required purification; softwood lignin in the cited work also required a plasticizing agent for melt-spinning.
Battery-material qualification with manufacturers and carmakers is reported to take 3 years in the company material; the evidence gives no product quality specification for the anode material.
The evidence says activated-carbon precursors have no strict quality limitations, while lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

limitations: The carbon-fiber precursor specifications are cited secondhand and do not apply to hard carbon or activated carbon; the study’s lignin was not from standard kraft pulping.
The older DOE carbon-fiber work’s mechanical properties were about 50% of its target; its targets are not precursor specifications.
The GreenLight summary is a project’s own report, its costs are modelled, and its TRL 5 applies to precursor-fiber spinning rather than the full carbon-fiber chain.
The hard-carbon feedstock comparison and kraft-lignin result are review summaries; the listed cost basis is not specified beyond $/t.
The activated-carbon work is laboratory-scale and uses zinc chloride activation.
The battery-material announcement is company investor material with forward-looking statements; its later status was not verified.

The feedstock profile does not establish ash, carbohydrate, volatile, or particulate compliance for carbon fiber, and the mill lacks fractionation/modification equipment and drying capability (feedstock:constraints[1], feedstock:constraints[2], feedstock:missing_properties[2]).
missing_information: No named commercial buyers, current regional demand, sales volumes, contracts, or current lignin prices are provided for these products.
The evidence does not establish commercial sales of Pinecrest-derived carbon fiber, hard carbon, or activated carbon.
The evidence does not provide Pinecrest measurements against carbon-fiber precursor specifications or customer acceptance specifications for hard carbon and activated carbon.
No current status is established for the announced anode-material pilot or its scale-up plans.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents development activity beyond laboratory studies, including precursor-fiber validation in an industrially relevant environment and a company-announced anode-material pilot with customer qualification activity; it does not document commercial sales.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin; the mill lacks chemical-modification equipment, so this would require new capability or an external processor.
The deterministic feedstock-compatibility check could not produce a score because there are no numeric requirements to compare with the feedstock.
Drying capability is needed if the buyer requires dry powder; Pinecrest currently has no lignin dryer and ships wet cake.
Scenario economics did not calculate product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or an indicative-economics score because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing.

technical_maturity.statement: The cited 2018 estimate places production of biobased phenolic resins at TRL 8; this is pathway-level evidence, not confirmation of Pinecrest-specific readiness.

adoption_barriers.statement: Diversion competes with the lignin's current internal-fuel use, and wet-cake shipment, variable moisture, and limited covered storage constrain supply logistics.

Plywood and wood-panel producers are identified customer types, but no named buyers, regional demand, purchase volumes, contracts, or current lignin price are provided; current commercial sales of kraft-lignin resin are not established by the supplied evidence.
The cited qualification evidence includes EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and EN 717-2 formaldehyde-emissions testing, so customer qualification and product testing remain adoption steps.

missing_inputs: Delivered Pinecrest cake composition and customer-specific acceptance data
Customer-specific product qualification and testing outcomes
assumptions: Scenario analysis uses fictional wet-feedstock-mass assumptions of 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr, moisture assumptions of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass, and availability fractions of 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0%.
No product yield, price, or variable-cost assumptions were supplied or imputed.
uncertainties: The feedstock's missing molecular-weight and phenolic-hydroxyl data and absent customer acceptance data could affect formulation suitability.
The evidence supports an industrially proven manufacturer application, but does not establish current commercial sales of kraft-lignin resin or Pinecrest-specific qualification.
The economics remain indicative only: the missing yield, price, and cost inputs prevent a contribution estimate.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: A plausible panel-adhesive application and a documented pretreatment route exist, but Pinecrest lacks chemical-modification and drying equipment, and no named buyer or commercial terms are established. Significant new processing capability and a commercial partner would therefore be needed.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 8 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-01#3.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon-fiber precursor, the deterministic feedstock-compatibility score is 1; the checked lignin-content and ash requirements are outside the feedstock limits reported by the compatibility check.

The cited carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm; the cited kraft lignin also required purification.
The cited work says a plasticizing agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin; Pinecrest has no fractionation or chemical-modification equipment and no lignin dryer.
For activated carbon, the evidence reports no strict precursor-quality limitations, while lower ash improves yield; this is a distinct, less stringent route than carbon-fiber precursor qualification.
Scenario economics did not calculate product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or an indicative-economics score because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing.

technical_maturity.statement: The cited GreenLight project raised lignin precursor-fiber production from TRL 2–3 to TRL 5 in an industrially relevant environment; this claim concerns precursor-fiber production, not all carbon-material routes.

adoption_barriers.statement: The compatibility result applies to the checked carbon-fiber precursor requirements; hard-carbon and activated-carbon customer specifications are not established in the supplied evidence, so the result should not be generalized across all carbon-material products.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Bio-based polyurethanes, including the small lignin-based share, hold less than 1% of the polyurethane market.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
